metadata.title: What Did Ancient Humans Actually Eat?

fragments.text: Open your fridge right now. A can of
soda, some yogurt, leftover pizza, and
maybe some fruit flown in from the other
side of the planet. But to your
ancestors, none of this is food. So,
what did they actually eat? The answer
would horrify most people alive today.
Scientists have found proof in caves
around the world. Proof that changes
everything we thought we knew about our
own species. But to understand it, we
have to go back to the beginning,
roughly 3 million years ago. Your
earliest ancestors were not hunters.
They were scavengers. When a lion killed
an antelope on the African savanna, it
ate parts first, the muscle, the liver,
the heart. Then the hyenas came in for
the rest, and they crunched through the
ribs, the skin, and the smaller bones.
By the time our ancestors got there,
what was left was scraps, thick leg
bones, bones too thick even for hyena
jaws to break. And this is what our
ancestors ate. Their signature meal was
bone marrow. Early humans would creep up
to a stripped carcass, grab the thickest
leg bones, and smash them open with
stone flakes called Oldowan tools.
Inside was marrow, gray, slick, dripping
fat. They scooped it out with their
fingers and ate it raw. For our
ancestors, this was a feast. No other
animal could get at it. The marrow was
sealed inside thick thigh bones, and we
had the one thing no other scavenger
had, hands that could grip a rock hard
enough to break them open. They ate the
brains, too. A cracked skull holds
almost a pound of solid fat, and fat is
the most calorie-dense food in the
animal. For an ancestor living on
scraps, a skull was a jackpot. This is
why your body still treats fat like
treasure. It still remembers. We also
ate insects, termites, grubs, beetles,
fat white larvae the size of your thumb.
They crunched like shrimp. For your deep
ancestors, insects were not a last
resort. They were dinner. This was life
for over a million years, day after day,
generation after generation. But what
came later is worse than you can
imagine. First, fire. The oldest human
fire we have ever found is inside
Wonderwerk Cave in South Africa. It is
about a million years old. Once we had
fire, we had cooking. Meat roasted over
coals, roots buried in hot ashes, marrow
bones dropped in the embers. Cooking is
pre-digestion. Raw meat and raw plants
force your gut to do hours of chemical
work to break them down. Cooked food is
already partly broken apart. Your body
spends less energy digesting it and
pulls more calories out of every bite.
And scientists believe that as our
ancestors started cooking, their guts
shrank. That freed up huge amounts of
energy, and it all went to one place,
the brain. It is only 2% of your body
weight, but uses 20% of your body's
calories. You cannot run that machine on
raw leaves and termites. You need
cooked, fat-rich food. Cooking gave us
our brains, and our brains gave us
everything else. That's when the menu
exploded. By 300,000 years ago, your
ancestors looked much like you do today,
and they were eating almost everything
they could catch, dig up, or reach.
Mammoth, bison, wild horse, and reindeer
on the plains. Fish and shellfish from
the rivers and coasts. Roots, wild
grains, berries, nuts, and mushrooms
from the land itself. Eggs stolen from
nests, and honey. Especially honey. The
Hadza, a hunter-gatherer tribe in
Tanzania, still eat the way humans ate
before farming existed. About 15% of
their calories come from wild honey.
They climb dangerous trees, get stung
hundreds of times, and keep going back
because nothing else in the wild packs
that many calories into one bite. And
here's what's strange, that exact same
craving is still alive in you today,
sugar. Your brain is wired for it
because for hundreds of thousands of
years, sugar gave your body two things
at once, instant energy to use right
now, and extra fuel your body stored as
fat. That fat was the only thing that
kept you alive when food ran out. A
dripping honeycomb was the richest meal
most of your ancestors ever laid eyes
on. This is the program running inside
you right now. Your body cannot tell the
difference between honey in a tree and a
donut. Modern food took that ancient
signal and turned it into a business.
Soda, candy, cereal, sauces, even most
bread. Almost every packaged food on
Earth is sugar wearing a different
costume. That is why you cannot stop
eating it. Your body is still trying to
store fat for the next time food runs
out. But sugar wasn't the only thing
your body got hooked on. So, what else
did your ancestors learn to crave? Meat.
A single mammoth carcass could feed a
tribe for weeks. One big kill saved
hundreds of hours that would otherwise
have been spent picking berries and
digging roots. That saved time became
time to raise children, teach skills,
make better tools, tell stories around
fires. This is why your body still
craves protein. Every craving you have
today was shaped by what kept them
alive. But there was one craving we
still have trouble admitting,
each other.
In a cave in England called Gough's
Cave, researchers found human bones from
about 14,700 years ago. And the bones
told a story no one wanted to read. The
skulls had been meticulously cleaned
with stone tools. The face and the base
had been carefully removed. What was
left was the top of the skull, shaped
rim by rim into a cup. The long bones
had been cracked open the same way your
earliest ancestors cracked open antelope
bones for the [snorts] marrow. And here
is where it gets worse. This wasn't
starvation. The same cave contains the
remains of horses, deer, and other
animals. There was plenty to eat. A 2017
study calculated how many calories a
human body actually provides. The answer
is around 125,000.
A single bison holds 600,000. A mammoth,
3 million. Humans weren't efficient
food. They were a choice. One forearm
bone found at Gough's Cave was carved
with a zigzag pattern after the meat was
gone. This wasn't a last resort. This
was a ritual. And Gough's Cave isn't the
only site. Similar remains have been
found across Europe at sites in Germany,
France, Spain, and Croatia. For hundreds
of thousands of years in different parts
of the world, humans were doing this to
each other, not always to survive.
Because somewhere in our history, we
decided it meant something. And it gets
stranger. Your ancestors didn't just eat
fresh meat. They ate rotten meat.
[music] When a hunter killed an animal,
they couldn't eat the whole thing at
once. So, they buried it, stashed it in
caves, hid it in cold streams for days,
for weeks, sometimes months. By the time
they came back, the meat was crawling
with maggots and reeked of decay. They
ate it anyway. Some researchers think
they even preferred it that way. Rotting
meat has already been partly broken down
by bacteria, easier to chew, easier to
absorb. The bacteria even produce B
vitamins your body needs. Your body
still remembers this. Every fermented
food you love is controlled rot. Cheese,
yogurt, sourdough, beer, wine, soy
sauce, pickles. They are all rot, slowed
down and made safe. Your taste for
cheese didn't develop in a French dairy.
It developed on a savanna 100,000 years
ago eating something far worse. Every
craving you have today for fat, for
salt, for sugar, for the richest thing
you can find, is still running inside
you right now. Your body doesn't know
about grocery stores or refrigerators.
It only knows this, eat what's rich, eat
what's rare, eat while you can, because
tomorrow there might be nothing. At
11:00 p.m., when you open the fridge
even though you're not hungry, you're
running a 3 million-year-old program,
still scanning, still trying to keep you
alive. But the world it was built for is
gone. If you took a modern human and
dropped them into the world of 50,000
years ago, they would probably die in
days. You would not know how to find
water. Half the plants would be a
mystery, and you would not be strong
enough to run down an animal, climb a
tree for honey, or crack open a thigh
bone for marrow. You would die staring
at a landscape full of food you could
not see. But if you dropped a
50,000-year-old human into your kitchen,
they would think they had walked into a
god's pantry. They would not understand
any of it. A cold, sweet drink sealed in
metal. Bread that someone else baked.
Milk that sat sealed and fresh for
weeks. Fruit from places they had never
heard of. Food that nobody had to chase.
It would look like the richest place
anyone had ever walked into. For 3
million years, every human who ever
lived was hungry, cold, and tired. You
might be the first one who isn't. And
you have no idea how rare that is.
